title: What machine learning is
text: Purpose. Before any formula, you need to know what problem machine learning solves and when it is the right tool. Every later technique hangs on this idea. Key ideas Ordinary software follows rules a person wrote. Machine learning finds the rules itself from examples. A model is a function that turns inputs into a prediction. Learning means choosing the numbers inside it (its parameters) so that its predictions match the examples. There are two phases: training (fit the parameters) and inference (use the fitted model on new inputs). Good data matters more than a clever algorithm.

title: 1.1 Rules versus examples
text: 1.1 Rules versus examples Imagine you must teach a new colleague to spot loan applications that will not be repaid. You have two options. The first is a rulebook: "decline if income is below X, or if the debt ratio is above Y". The second is to hand over 10,000 past files with their outcomes and let them develop a feel for it. Machine learning is the second option, done by a computer. Arthur Samuel gave the classic definition in 1959: machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. His checkers program played tens of thousands of games against itself and ended up playing better than he did (Ng, video 3). Nobody wrote its strategy. It found one. This matters because some problems have too many rules to write. Nobody can list the rules that separate spam from real mail, recognise a voice, or rank web pages. For those problems, examples work and rulebooks do not.

title: 1.2 A model is a small picture of the world
text: 1.2 A model is a small picture of the world When you see dark clouds and predict rain, you are using a mental model. A model in machine learning is the same thing written as a function: inputs go in, a prediction comes out. The simplest useful one is a straight line: The numbers m and b are the parameters. They decide whether the predictions are any good. "Learning" is the search for the m and b that fit the examples best (Shaw Talebi, ML Foundations).

title: 1.3 Training and inference
text: 1.3 Training and inference Phase What happens Cost Analogy Training The parameters are fitted to example data Slow, done once or now and then Going to school Inference The fitted model predicts for a new input Fast, done all the time Doing the job When people say a model "costs" a lot, they usually mean training. When your app answers a customer, that is inference.

title: 1.4 Three ways to learn
text: 1.4 Three ways to learn Supervised learning: every example comes with the right answer. The model learns to map inputs to answers. Most business ML is this. Unsupervised learning: there are no answers. The model looks for structure by itself, such as groups of similar customers. Reinforcement learning: the model tries actions and gets a reward or a penalty. It learns by trial and error. AlphaGo used it, and so did the training of reasoning models such as DeepSeek R1, which were rewarded for correct maths and code answers. Chapter 2 covers all three in detail. Deep learning is not a fourth way to learn. It is a kind of model, a neural network with many layers, that can be trained in any of the three ways, most often the first.

title: 1.5 AI, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs
text: 1.5 AI, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs These terms nest like Russian dolls. Artificial intelligence is the broad goal. Machine learning is the part of it that learns from data. Deep learning is the part of machine learning that uses large neural networks. A large language model (LLM) is a deep network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word, then refined with supervised examples and reinforcement learning. This book moves in that order: classical machine learning first, because LLMs reuse its ideas.

title: 1.6 Where machine learning is used
text: 1.6 Where machine learning is used You already use it many times a day: web search ranking, tagging friends in photos, movie recommendations, voice assistants and spam filters. In industry it optimizes wind turbines, helps doctors diagnose, and inspects products on factory lines with computer vision (Ng, videos 1 and 2). Ng quotes McKinsey's estimate that AI and machine learning could add about $13 trillion of value per year by 2030, much of it outside software: retail, travel, transport and manufacturing. He also says artificial general intelligence, machines as smart as people, is overhyped and still far away.

title: 1.7 When not to use machine learning
text: 1.7 When not to use machine learning Beyond the videos. Machine learning is not always the answer: If the rule is clear and stable, write the rule. "The borrower must be 18 or older" is a rule, not a prediction. If you have no data, or only a handful of examples, a model has nothing to learn from. If a wrong prediction is very costly and nobody can explain it, you need extra safeguards, or a simpler model. Always try a trivial baseline first (Chapter 3). If a clever model barely beats it, the clever model is not worth its cost.

title: 1.8 The workflow in one list
text: 1.8 The workflow in one list Define the problem as a prediction: what is the input, and what is the answer? Collect and clean the data. Choose the inputs (features) and how to prepare them (Chapter 8). Train a model (Chapters 4 to 7, 9 and 10). Evaluate it on data it has never seen (Chapters 3 and 12). Deploy it, watch it, and retrain when the world changes. Loan example. Rules handle the legal checks: is the applicant of age, is the amount within the product limit. A model handles the questions with no clean rule: "how likely is this applicant to accept our offer?" and "what will this offer cost per month?" The first needs a classifier (Chapter 9), the second a regression (Chapter 7). Common mistakes Using machine learning where a rule would do, and then having to maintain a model nobody can explain. Judging a model by how well it does on the data it was trained on (Chapter 3). Spending weeks on the algorithm when the data is wrong. Check yourself Explain the difference between a rule-based system and a machine learning system, using a loan example. Name the two phases of a model's life and say which one is expensive. Is deep learning a way to learn, like supervised learning? Explain. Give one task in a bank where you would write a rule instead of training a model. Show answers (1) A rule-based system applies rules a person wrote; a learning system finds the pattern from past files and their outcomes. (2) Training and inference; training is the expensive one. (3) No. It is a type of model that can be trained in any of the three ways. (4) For example checking that an applicant is of legal age. title: The map of machine learning
text: Purpose. When you meet a new technique, you should know which family it belongs to and what kind of problem it solves. This chapter is the map. Later chapters fill in the territory. Key ideas Supervised learning learns from examples with the right answer. Its two tasks are regression (predict a number) and classification (predict a category). Unsupervised learning has no answers and finds structure: clusters, unusual cases, simpler descriptions. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards by trial and error. The first question to ask about any problem is: do I have the right answers for past cases? Read the map from left to right. Machine learning splits into three ways to learn, each into types, each with its models. Course 1 of Ng's specialization starts at the highlighted Regression box. Course 2 adds neural networks and trees, and course 3 adds clustering, anomaly detection and reinforcement learning.

title: 2.1 Supervised learning
text: 2.1 Supervised learning In supervised learning each training example is a pair: an input x and the right answer y (the label). The algorithm learns the mapping from x to y, so that it can predict y for an input it has never seen. Ng says that about 99% of the economic value created by machine learning today comes from this family. It comes in two tasks: Regression predicts a number from infinitely many possible values. A house price from its size. A monthly loan cost from the amount and the term. Classification predicts a category from a small set. Spam or not spam. A tumour that is benign (0) or malignant (1). The classes need not be numbers (cat or dog), and there can be more than two (Gmail's tabs: primary, social, promotions). With two inputs, the algorithm draws a boundary line between the classes.

title: 2.2 Unsupervised learning
text: 2.2 Unsupervised learning The data has inputs only. Nobody tells the algorithm what the answers are, so it looks for structure by itself. Ng's examples: Google News puts articles that share words (panda, twins, zoo) into one group; researchers group people by DNA activity; DeepLearning.AI found three learner segments (growing skills, developing a career, staying updated). The three main tasks: Clustering: group similar examples. Anomaly detection: find unusual examples, such as fraud. Dimensionality reduction: compress many features into a few while keeping most of the information.

title: 2.3 Reinforcement learning
text: 2.3 Reinforcement learning An agent takes actions in an environment and receives rewards or penalties. It learns which actions earn the most reward over time. Famous examples: checkers (Samuel), Go (AlphaGo), and the training of reasoning LLMs, which were rewarded for correct answers. It is rare in lending, because you cannot let a model try random loans to see what happens, but it matters for understanding how modern LLMs are made.

title: 2.4 Side by side
text: 2.4 Side by side Supervised Unsupervised Reinforcement The data Inputs x with right answers y Inputs x only An environment that gives rewards The goal Learn x to y, then predict y for a new x Find groups, patterns, oddities Choose actions that earn the most reward Tasks Regression, classification Clustering, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction Control, games, tuning LLMs Loan example Monthly cost of an offer (regression); offer accepted or not (classification) Applicant segments; an unusual application Rare; a pricing policy learned from simulation

title: 2.5 Choosing the family
text: 2.5 Choosing the family Question Answer Family and task Do I have the right answers for past cases? Yes, and the answer is a number Supervised, regression Yes, and the answer is a category Supervised, classification No, and I want groups Unsupervised, clustering No, and I want the odd ones out Unsupervised, anomaly detection No, and I have too many columns Unsupervised, dimensionality reduction Must it choose actions and learn from their results? Yes Reinforcement learning Quick tests from Ng's quiz: spam filtering and diabetes prediction are supervised (the answers are known); grouping news articles and finding market segments are unsupervised.

title: 2.6 Self-supervised learning
text: 2.6 Self-supervised learning Beyond the videos. There is a fourth label you will meet when reading about LLMs: self-supervised learning. The training data comes with no human labels, but the labels are made from the data itself. An LLM reads a sentence with the next word hidden and learns to predict it. The "right answer" is simply the next word of the text. This lets models learn from the entire internet without anyone labelling it. Loan example. A table of 40,000 past offers with a column Accepted (yes or no) is supervised classification data. The same table without that column can still be clustered into customer types, but the groups come with no names and you must interpret them. Common mistakes Calling a clustering result a classification. Clustering has no known classes. It invents groups, and you give them meaning afterwards. Using regression for a yes or no question just because the labels are 0 and 1 (Chapter 9 explains why that goes wrong). Check yourself Is "predict whether a customer repays" regression or classification? Why? Is "find groups of similar loan applicants" supervised or unsupervised? Give one loan example of anomaly detection. What is the label in supervised learning? Show answers (1) Classification: the answer is a category (repays or not). (2) Unsupervised: there is no right answer to learn from. (3) Flagging an application whose pattern differs from all previous ones, as a fraud check. (4) The right answer y that comes with each training example. title: Data and the vocabulary
text: Purpose. Nearly every formula in this book uses the same few symbols. Learn them once here. Also learn why data quality and honest testing matter more than any algorithm. Key ideas A dataset is a table. A row is one example, a column is one feature, and one special column is the target (the label). Parameters are learned by training. Hyperparameters are chosen by you before training. Always test on data the model never saw. Split the data into training, validation and test sets. Before building a model, measure a trivial baseline. A model that does not beat it is useless.

title: 3.1 A dataset is a table
text: 3.1 A dataset is a table Here are five rows of a loan-offers table. The values are made up for illustration. # OfferedAmount (EUR) NumberOfTerms CreditScore Accepted (target) 1 10,000 36 720 1 2 25,000 60 650 0 3 5,000 24 780 1 4 40,000 84 600 0 5 15,000 48 690 1 Columns 1 to 3 are the inputs (features). The last column is what you want to predict (the target, or label). Each row is one training example. A model learns from the rows where the target is known, and is then used on new rows where it is not.

title: 3.2 Notation
text: 3.2 Notation Symbol Meaning In the table above m number of training examples 5 n number of features 3 x the input features the first three columns y the target, the true answer the Accepted column (x^(i), y^(i)) the i-th training example (the superscript is a row number, not a power) row 2: x^(2) = [25000, 60, 650], y^(2) = 0 x^(i)_j feature j of example i x^(2)_3 = 650 f(x) or y-hat the model's prediction what the model says for a row w, b the parameters (weights and bias) learned by training A vector is just a list of numbers. x^(2) is the vector of all features of the second row.

title: 3.3 Parameters and hyperparameters
text: 3.3 Parameters and hyperparameters Parameters are the numbers the algorithm learns: w and b in a line, the weights in a neural network. Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training and that training does not change: the learning rate, the number of passes over the data (epochs), K in nearest neighbours, the regularization strength, the polynomial degree. You find good hyperparameters by trying values and measuring on held-out data, not by guessing (Shaw Talebi).

title: 3.4 Train, validation and test sets
text: 3.4 Train, validation and test sets A model that scores well on the examples it was fitted to has proved nothing, just as a student who sees the exam questions in advance proves nothing. You need data the model has never seen: Set Used for Typical share Training fitting the parameters 60 to 80% Validation choosing hyperparameters and comparing models 10 to 20% Test one final honest score, used once at the end 10 to 20% Two rules that save careers. First, fit any preparation step (such as scaling) on the training set only , then apply it to the others. Fitting it on everything lets information from the test rows leak into training. Second, for data that has a time order, such as loans, split by date : train on the past, test on the future. A random split lets the model peek at the future and flatters it. Chapter 12 goes deeper.

title: 3.5 Data quality
text: 3.5 Data quality Machine learning is only as good as its data: garbage in, garbage out. Good data has quantity (too few examples lead to overfitting, Chapter 11) and quality (Shaw Talebi): Accurate. An age of 35 that should be 53, or an income of $12,000 that is really per month, teaches the model something false. Diverse and representative. A churn model trained only on Pro users will fail on Enterprise customers. Beyond the videos. Three traps that are especially common in lending: Selection bias. You only know whether people repaid if you approved them. A model trained on approved loans has never seen the rejected ones. Leakage. A feature that is only known after the outcome, such as a collections status, makes a model look brilliant in testing and useless in production. Always ask: would I have this value at the moment of the decision? Label noise. The target itself can be wrong or defined inconsistently, for example "default" meaning 60 days late in one system and 90 in another.

title: 3.6 Always measure a baseline
text: 3.6 Always measure a baseline A baseline is the simplest sensible prediction: for regression, predict the average of the training targets; for classification, predict the most common class. If 95% of offers are accepted, a model that always says "accepted" is 95% accurate and completely useless. Your model has to beat the baseline by a margin that matters, or it is not earning its complexity. Loan example. In the table above, three of five offers are accepted (60%). A baseline that always predicts "accepted" is right 60% of the time. Any classifier you build on this table must beat 60%, measured on rows it did not train on. Common mistakes Scoring a model on its training data, and then being surprised in production. Scaling or cleaning the whole dataset before splitting it (leakage). Random-splitting time-ordered data. Skipping the baseline. Check yourself In the offers table, what are m and n, and what is x^(3)? What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter? Give an example of each. Why must a test set be used only once, at the end? Give an example of leakage in a loan model. Show answers (1) m = 5, n = 3, x^(3) = [5000, 24, 780]. (2) A parameter is learned (a weight w); a hyperparameter is chosen by you (the learning rate). (3) If you tune on it, it stops being unseen data and the score becomes too optimistic. (4) Using "days in collections" to predict default: you only know it after the default has started. Go deeper: Google's Rules of Machine Learning (practical, written by engineers) · the scikit-learn pages on cross-validation and preprocessing · An Introduction to Statistical Learning , free book .

title: Linear regression with one feature
text: Purpose. A straight line through data is the simplest model that learns. Logistic regression, neural networks and even LLMs are variations on it, so understand this one fully. Key ideas The model is f(x) = w x + b. The weight w is the slope and the bias b is the value at x = 0. "Best line" has to be defined. The usual definition: the line that makes the squared gaps to the points as small as possible. You can find that line in one step with a formula (least squares), or step by step with gradient descent (Chapter 6). With one input feature the model is called univariate linear regression.

title: 4.1 The model
text: 4.1 The model Ng's running example predicts a house price from its size, using 47 houses from Portland. Plot size on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, and the points rise to the right. Draw a line through them and you can read off a price for any size: his client's 1,250 square foot house comes out at about $250,000. x is the input (size), and f(x) , written y-hat, is the prediction (price). w (weight, slope, coefficient): how much the prediction rises when x rises by 1. b (bias, intercept): the prediction when x is 0. With w = 0.2 thousand dollars per square foot and b = 0, a 1,250 square foot house gives 1,250 x 0.2 = 250, which is $250,000. Different values of w and b give different lines, and training is the search for the best pair.

title: 4.2 What "best" means
text: 4.2 What "best" means A line can pass close to some points and far from others. To compare lines you need one number that says how far a line is from all the points together. The recipe (Infinite Codes asks you to put each formula into words like this): For one point, the error is the prediction minus the true value: f(x) - y. Square it, so that errors above and below the line both count as positive, and big misses count much more than small ones. Add up the squares over all points. Take three points (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3). The line with w = 1 and b = 0 passes through all three: every error is 0. The line with w = 0.5 and b = 0 predicts 0.5, 1 and 1.5, so the errors are -0.5, -1 and -1.5. Squared and added, that is 0.25 + 1 + 2.25 = 3.5. The first line is clearly better, and the number says so. Chapter 5 turns this recipe into the cost function.

title: 4.3 Two ways to find the best line
text: 4.3 Two ways to find the best line A formula (least squares, the normal equation). For linear regression only, calculus gives w and b directly, with no repeated steps. Libraries such as NumPy and scikit-learn use it. Gradient descent. Start anywhere and improve step by step. It is slower here, but it also works for logistic regression and neural networks, where no formula exists. Code: the formula. Fifty noisy points around the line y = 3x + 2: import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(0) x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 50) y = 3 * x + 2 + rng.normal(0, 1, 50) A = np.c_[x, np.ones_like(x)] # a column of x and a column of ones (for b) w, b = np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0] print(round(w, 3), round(b, 3)) # 3.052 1.757 print(round(w * 4 + b, 2)) # prediction for x = 4: 13.97 The true values are 3 and 2. The fit finds 3.052 and 1.757, because the noise nudges it. The same data is reused in Chapter 6.

title: 4.4 Using a fitted line well
text: 4.4 Using a fitted line well Beyond the videos. Interpolation is safe, extrapolation is not. The line is only trustworthy inside the range of sizes it saw. A line fitted to houses between 300 and 2,000 square feet says little about a 10,000 square foot mansion. Correlation is not causation. A good fit tells you that size and price move together, not that making a house bigger would raise its value by the slope. Mind the units. If x is in square feet and y in thousands of dollars, w is in thousands of dollars per square foot. A weight is meaningless without its units. Loan example. Predict the monthly cost of an offer from the offered amount. A fitted model might look like f(amount) = 0.029 x amount + 8 (invented numbers). Then a 10,000 euro offer is predicted at 0.029 x 10,000 + 8 = 298 euros per month. Once you add the number of terms as a second input (Chapter 7), the predictions get much better. Common mistakes Reading w as "the effect of x" without checking the units or the range. Predicting far outside the range of the training inputs. Forgetting that b exists: a model f(x) = w x forces the line through the origin. Check yourself For f(x) = 0.2 x + 30, what is the prediction at x = 100, and what does 30 mean? Why do we square the errors instead of just adding them? Why can we not trust a fitted line far outside the data it saw? Show answers (1) 0.2 x 100 + 30 = 50; 30 is the prediction at x = 0, the bias. (2) Plain errors above and below the line cancel each other, and squaring also punishes big misses. (3) The relationship may change outside that range, and the data has no evidence about it. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 9 and 10 · the scikit-learn linear models guide · An Introduction to Statistical Learning , chapter 3 (free book, statlearning.com ).

title: The cost function
text: Purpose. A computer cannot look at a plot and say "that line looks good". It needs one number that measures how wrong a line is, and the training task becomes making that number small. Key ideas The cost J(w, b) is the average squared error, with a factor 1/2 that tidies later maths. A lower cost means a better fit, so training means minimizing J. J as a function of w and b is a bowl. The bottom of the bowl is the best line. Squared error for linear regression gives a bowl with a single bottom (convex), so there are no traps.

title: 5.1 The formula
text: 5.1 The formula Read it from the inside out: the error of example i, squared, added over all m examples, divided by m to get an average (so that the number does not grow just because you have more data), and divided by 2 as well. The extra 2 does nothing to the answer: it only cancels the 2 that appears when you take the derivative in Chapter 6.

title: 5.2 A worked example
text: 5.2 A worked example Use the three points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) and fix b = 0, so the cost depends only on w. For w = 0.5: J = 1 / (2 x 3) x ( (0.5 - 1)^2 + (1 - 2)^2 + (1.5 - 3)^2 ) = (0.25 + 1 + 2.25) / 6 = 0.583 w The line Cost J(w) 1 Goes through every point 0 0.5 Too flat 0.583 0 Flat at zero 2.333 Plot cost against w and you get a parabola (a U shape) whose lowest point is at w = 1. The goal of linear regression is to find the w and b that sit at the bottom. import numpy as np x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) def cost(w, b): return np.sum((w * x + b - y) ** 2) / (2 * len(x)) print(cost(1, 0), round(cost(0.5, 0), 3), round(cost(0, 0), 3)) # 0.0 0.583 2.333

title: 5.3 Seeing the bowl
text: 5.3 Seeing the bowl With both w and b free, J is a surface over a plane: a bowl, like a soup bowl or a hammock. A contour plot shows the same bowl from above, like a topographic map: every ring is a set of (w, b) pairs with the same cost, and the centre is the minimum. In Ng's housing example a point far from the centre (w about -0.15, b about 800) is a very bad line, while points near the centre fit well. Reading such plots by hand does not scale, so we need an algorithm that walks to the centre by itself. That is gradient descent.

title: 5.4 Convex: one bottom, no traps
text: 5.4 Convex: one bottom, no traps The squared-error cost of linear regression is convex : one bowl, one lowest point, no side valleys. Wherever you start, going downhill ends at the global minimum. The cost surface of a neural network is not convex. It has many valleys (local minima), and where training ends depends on where it started.

title: 5.5 Other ways to measure error
text: 5.5 Other ways to measure error Beyond the videos. The squared error is the standard choice, but there are others, and you will meet these names: Measure Formula in words Notes MSE (mean squared error) average of the squared errors the cost J without the 1/2: here 2 x 0.583 = 1.167 RMSE square root of the MSE same units as y, so easier to explain: 1.08 here MAE (mean absolute error) average of the absolute errors treats all errors alike, less hurt by outliers R squared 1 minus (error around the fit) / (error around the mean) 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than always guessing the average A bank manager understands "typically wrong by 22 euros a month" (RMSE) better than "mean squared error 480". Loan example. Take the monthly cost of each offer. The cost J measures how far, on average and squared, the predicted monthly cost is from the real one. One outlier offer with a 500 euro error adds as much squared error as 25 offers with a 100 euro error. Check whether that is what you want, because it decides whether MSE or MAE suits the business. Common mistakes Comparing the cost of two models on different datasets, or one on training and one on test data. Forgetting that the cost depends on the units of y. A cost of 480 is large for prices in dollars and tiny for prices in cents. Believing a low cost proves the model is good. It might simply fit the training data too closely (Chapter 11). Check yourself Compute J for the points (1, 2), (2, 4) and w = 2, b = 0. Why divide by m? Why divide by 2? What does convex mean, and why is it good news? Show answers (1) The line predicts 2 and 4, the errors are 0, so J = 0. (2) Dividing by m makes the cost an average that does not depend on the amount of data; the 2 only cancels the 2 from the derivative. (3) The cost has one bottom and no false valleys, so downhill always ends at the best solution. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 11 to 14 · Google's Linear regression module in the crash course · the scikit-learn page on model evaluation for the other error measures.

title: Gradient descent
text: Purpose. Gradient descent is the general way to minimize a cost. It trains linear regression, logistic regression and the largest neural networks. If you understand it, you understand how almost every model in this book learns. Key ideas Start with any w and b, then repeatedly take a small step downhill on the cost. The step direction comes from the derivative (the slope). The step size is set by the learning rate alpha. Update all parameters at the same time. Alpha too small is slow. Alpha too large overshoots and can make the cost grow. The learning curve (cost against iterations) tells you whether training works.

title: 6.1 The idea
text: 6.1 The idea Imagine you are walking down a dark valley with a torch that lights only your feet. You cannot see the bottom, but you can feel which way the ground slopes. So you take a small step in the steepest downhill direction, feel the slope again, and repeat. Ng's picture is a hilly golf course: stand on a hill, turn all the way round, take a baby step in the steepest downhill direction, repeat. You end up at the bottom of a valley.

title: 6.2 The update rule
text: 6.2 The update rule The sign := means "assign", as in code. It is not a claim that both sides are equal. alpha is the learning rate, a small positive number such as 0.01. It sets the size of each step. The derivative is the slope of the cost in that direction. If the slope is positive (uphill to the right), subtracting it moves w to the left. If the slope is negative, w moves right. Either way you move towards the bottom. Update w and b simultaneously: compute both new values from the old ones first, then assign them. Updating w first and then using the new w to compute b's step is a subtle bug. When you reach the minimum the slope is 0, so the update changes nothing: the algorithm has converged. Even with a fixed alpha, the steps shrink on their own near the bottom because the slope shrinks.

title: 6.3 The derivatives for linear regression
text: 6.3 The derivatives for linear regression Calculus gives (Ng, video 19): In words: the step for b is the average error. The step for w is the average of the error times the input, so examples with large inputs have more say about w. The 2 from differentiating the square cancels the 1/2 in the cost.

title: 6.4 A worked example, by hand
text: 6.4 A worked example, by hand Take the three points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), start at w = 0, b = 0, and use alpha = 0.1. Predictions: 0, 0, 0. Errors f - y: -1, -2, -3. The cost is 2.333. dJ/dw = (1/3) x (-1 x 1 + -2 x 2 + -3 x 3) = -14/3 = -4.667. dJ/db = (1/3) x (-1 - 2 - 3) = -2. New w = 0 - 0.1 x (-4.667) = 0.467. New b = 0 - 0.1 x (-2) = 0.2. The new cost is 0.470, down from 2.333. Repeating gives, after steps 2, 3, 4, 5: w = 0.676, 0.770, 0.813, 0.833 and costs 0.101, 0.027, 0.012, 0.009. After 2,000 steps it reaches w = 1.0 and b = 0.0. The cost falls fastest at the start, when the slope is steepest, and then crawls.

title: 6.5 Code from scratch
text: 6.5 Code from scratch Same fifty points as in Chapter 4: import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(0) x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 50) y = 3 * x + 2 + rng.normal(0, 1, 50) def gradient_descent(x, y, alpha, steps): w, b = 0.0, 0.0 history = [] for _ in range(steps): err = w * x + b - y # prediction minus target, for every example dw = (err * x).mean() # both derivatives use the OLD w and b db = err.mean() w, b = w - alpha * dw, b - alpha * db # simultaneous update history.append((err ** 2).mean() / 2) # cost before this step return w, b, history w, b, history = gradient_descent(x, y, alpha=0.05, steps=500) print(round(w, 3), round(b, 3)) # 3.053 1.753 (the formula gave 3.052 1.757) Gradient descent lands within 0.004 of the exact answer from the formula.

title: 6.6 Choosing the learning rate
text: 6.6 Choosing the learning rate On this data, after 500 steps: Alpha Result What it means 0.001 w = 3.220, b = 0.613 Still moving: too small, too slow 0.01 w = 3.112, b = 1.350 Closer, still not there 0.05 w = 3.053, b = 1.753 Converged 0.1 w grows without bound Too large: each step overshoots further than the last If the learning rate is too large, a step jumps over the bottom and lands higher on the other side, then jumps back even further. The cost grows on every step. If it is too small, training is correct but you may wait forever.

title: 6.7 Is it working? The learning curve
text: 6.7 Is it working? The learning curve Plot the cost J after every iteration (not against w or b). This is the learning curve (Ng, video 27). If gradient descent works, J goes down on every single iteration. If J ever goes up, alpha is too large, or there is a bug. A classic bug is writing w + alpha x slope instead of minus. When the curve flattens, training has converged. The number of iterations needed can be 30 for one problem and 100,000 for another, so you cannot know in advance. An automatic test: stop when J falls by less than a tiny epsilon (such as 0.001) in one iteration. Ng finds it hard to choose epsilon, so he prefers to look at the graph. Debugging tip: set alpha to a very small number. J must then fall on every iteration. If it does not, the code has a bug. A tiny alpha is for debugging, not for real training. Choosing alpha: try values about three times apart: 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1. Run a few iterations of each, plot the curves, and pick the largest value that still falls steadily, or one slightly smaller.

title: 6.8 Batch, stochastic and mini-batch
text: 6.8 Batch, stochastic and mini-batch Beyond the videos. The version above uses all m examples for every step. That is batch gradient descent (Ng, video 20). For millions of examples it is slow, so practitioners compute the slope on a random small group of examples per step: stochastic gradient descent uses one example, mini-batch uses a few (often 32 to 256). Steps become noisier, but far cheaper, and the model still converges. Neural networks are almost always trained with mini-batches and an improved version of gradient descent called Adam, which adapts the step size for each parameter. Loan example. Training the monthly-cost model from a table of offers is exactly this loop: predict, measure the gap to the real monthly cost, compute the two slopes, nudge w and b, repeat until the learning curve is flat. Common mistakes Updating w and b one after the other instead of simultaneously. Choosing alpha by a single guess and never plotting the learning curve. Plus instead of minus in the update. Running gradient descent on unscaled features and wondering why it is slow (Chapter 8). Check yourself A slope is positive. In which direction does w move, and why? You see the cost going up and down on successive iterations. Name two possible causes. Why does gradient descent slow down near the minimum even if alpha does not change? Do one step by hand for the points (1, 2), (2, 4) from w = 0, b = 0 with alpha = 0.1. What are w and b afterwards? Show answers (1) w moves left, to smaller values, because w := w - alpha x slope and the slope is positive. (2) Alpha is too large (overshooting), or a bug such as a sign error. (3) The slope shrinks as you approach the bottom, so each step is smaller. (4) Errors are -2 and -4; dw = (1/2)(-2 x 1 + -4 x 2) = -5, db = (1/2)(-2 - 4) = -3; so w = 0.5 and b = 0.3. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 15 to 20 and 27 to 28 · 3Blue1Brown's neural network series has the best animation of gradient descent (chapter 2) · Stanford CS229 lecture notes , first chapters (more maths).

title: Many features, and vectorization
text: Purpose. Real problems have many inputs: a house has a size, rooms, floors and an age; an offer has an amount, a term and a credit score. This chapter extends the line to many features and shows how to compute with all of them at once, which is what makes machine learning fast enough to be useful. Key ideas With n features the model has one weight per feature and one bias: f(x) = w1 x1 + ... + wn xn + b = w . x + b. The dot product multiplies matching pairs and adds them up. It is the core operation of machine learning. Vectorization means doing that arithmetic on whole arrays at once (NumPy). It is shorter and hundreds of times faster than a Python loop. Gradient descent works the same as before, with one slope per weight.

title: 7.1 The model with several features
text: 7.1 The model with several features Ng's house now has four features: size x1, bedrooms x2, floors x3 and age x4. The notation: n is the number of features, x_j is feature j, and x^(i) is the list (vector) of all features of example i. The second house in his table is x^(2) = [1416, 3, 2, 40], and x^(2)_3 = 2 is its number of floors. The model gives each feature its own weight. Ng's example prices a house in thousands of dollars: b = 80: a base price of $80,000 before size, rooms and age. 0.1 on size: every extra square foot adds 0.1 thousand dollars, $100. 4 on bedrooms, 10 on floors: +$4,000 per bedroom and +$10,000 per floor. -2 on age: every year of age takes $2,000 off. For the second house the model predicts 0.1 x 1416 + 4 x 3 + 10 x 2 - 2 x 40 + 80 = 173.6, so $173,600. Each weight says how much the prediction changes when that feature rises by one unit, with all the other features held fixed . That last phrase matters when features move together (see 7.6).

title: 7.2 The dot product
text: 7.2 The dot product Write all weights as a vector w and all features as a vector x. The dot product of two lists of the same length multiplies the matching pairs and adds the results, so the long formula collapses into one short one: Example: w = [2, 3], x = [10, 4], b = 5. The dot product is 2 x 10 + 3 x 4 = 32, and adding b gives 37. This model, with several features and a straight-line combination of them, is called multiple linear regression . (Ng points out that "multivariate regression" means something different, so avoid that name.)

title: 7.3 Vectorization
text: 7.3 Vectorization In Python you can compute the prediction three ways. NumPy counts from 0, so the first weight is w[0]. import numpy as np w, x = np.array([2, 3]), np.array([10, 4]) total = 0 for j in range(len(w)): # 1. a loop: one step after another total += w[j] * x[j] print(total + 5, np.dot(w, x) + 5, w @ x + 5) # 37 37 37 (loop, np.dot, the @ operator) Writing every term by hand (w[0]*x[0] + w[1]*x[1] + ...) works for 3 features and is impossible for 100,000. The loop works but is slow. np.dot(w, x) is the vectorized form: one line, and far faster. Two benefits (Ng, video 22): the code is shorter and easier to read, and it runs much faster, because NumPy hands the work to compiled code and parallel hardware (the CPU's vector units, or a GPU) that multiplies all the pairs at the same time instead of one after another (video 23). On one run on my laptop, a million multiplications took 0.116 seconds in a Python loop and 0.00015 seconds with np.dot , about 750 times faster. The exact ratio changes from machine to machine; the gap does not. The same trick updates all weights in gradient descent: instead of 16 separate lines, w = w - 0.1 * d updates all 16 at once. With thousands of features and a large dataset, this is the difference between one minute and many hours.

title: 7.4 Gradient descent with many features
text: 7.4 Gradient descent with many features The algorithm is the same as Chapter 6. For every weight there is one slope, and every weight is updated at the same time: Compared with one feature, only the last factor changes: it is feature j of each example, instead of the single x. Putting all examples in a matrix X with m rows and n columns makes the code short: def gradient_descent(X, y, alpha, steps): m, n = X.shape w, b = np.zeros(n), 0.0 history = [] for _ in range(steps): err = X @ w + b - y # all m errors at once w = w - alpha * (X.T @ err) / m # all n weight updates at once b = b - alpha * err.mean() history.append((err ** 2).mean() / 2) return w, b, np.array(history) There are no loops over features or examples. Chapter 8 runs it on real-looking data.

title: 7.5 The normal equation
text: 7.5 The normal equation For linear regression only, w and b can be computed directly, with no iterations. This is the normal equation . Ng's advice: do not implement it yourself, and know that it does not generalize to logistic regression or neural networks and gets slow when the number of features is very large. But many libraries, including scikit-learn's LinearRegression , solve linear regression this way behind the scenes. If an interviewer says "normal equation", this is what they mean. Beyond the videos. In practice you call np.linalg.lstsq (as in Chapter 4) rather than invert a matrix yourself, because inverting can be numerically unstable. The formula is singular when two features are exact copies of each other.

title: 7.6 The statistics view
text: 7.6 The statistics view StatQuest's multiple regression video (5 minutes) shows how statisticians look at the same model. Multiple regression fits a plane, or a higher-dimensional shape, instead of a line. The extra dimensions are just more columns of data. R squared works the same way as before: it compares the errors around the fitted line with the errors around the mean. Adding any feature can only make R squared rise a little, so use adjusted R squared , which corrects for the extra parameters. Counting parameters. The tests need the number of parameters that least squares estimates: the mean alone has 1, a simple regression has 2, a regression with two features has 3. Is the extra feature worth it? Compare the simple fit with the multiple fit. If R squared improves by a lot and the p-value is small, collecting the extra feature was worth the trouble. Beyond the videos. Watch out when features are strongly correlated with each other, such as height in centimetres and height in inches, or loan amount and monthly cost. The model can still predict well, but the individual weights become unstable and hard to interpret, because there are many ways to split the effect between them. This is called multicollinearity. Loan example. Predict the monthly cost of an offer from two features: x1 is the offered amount and x2 is the number of terms. The model is monthly cost = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + b, with two weights and one bias. Loading the offers table, building X with two columns and calling the function above is the whole exercise. Common mistakes Looping over features in Python when one @ or np.dot does it. Reading a weight as the effect of a feature without remembering "all else fixed". Adding features until the training score looks perfect (Chapter 11 explains why that backfires). Mixing up shapes: X is m by n, w has n entries, err has m entries. Check yourself With n = 4 features, how many parameters does the model learn? Compute w . x + b for w = [1, 2, 3], x = [4, 5, 6], b = -10. Give two reasons that np.dot beats a for loop. Why is the normal equation not enough for the rest of the course? Show answers (1) Five: four weights and the bias. (2) 4 + 10 + 18 - 10 = 22. (3) Shorter code, and much faster because it uses compiled code and parallel hardware. (4) It only works for linear regression, while logistic regression and neural networks have no such formula. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 21 to 24 · StatQuest, Multiple Regression, Clearly Explained · the NumPy quickstart · optionally 3Blue1Brown, Dot products and duality .

title: Preparing features
text: Purpose. A model only sees the numbers you give it. The same data, rescaled or combined in a smarter way, can train in 70 steps instead of never, and can fit a curve with a linear model. This chapter is about turning raw columns into good inputs. Key ideas Features on very different scales make gradient descent slow. Rescale them to similar ranges, roughly -1 to +1. Fit the scaling on the training data only and reuse its numbers for new data. Feature engineering builds new inputs from old ones: ratios, products, powers, dates, one-hot columns. Adding powers of a feature (x, x squared, x cubed) lets a linear model fit a curve. Scaling then matters even more.

title: 8.1 Why scaling matters
text: 8.1 Why scaling matters Suppose size runs from 300 to 2,000 square feet and bedrooms from 0 to 5. Take a 2,000 sq ft house with 5 bedrooms that costs $500k (Ng, video 25): w1 = 50, w2 = 0.1, b = 50 predicts 50 x 2000 + 0.1 x 5 + 50, over $100 million. Terrible. w1 = 0.1, w2 = 50, b = 50 predicts 0.1 x 2000 + 50 x 5 + 50 = 500, which is $500k. Right. So a feature with a big range ends up with a small weight, and a feature with a small range ends up with a big weight. That has a consequence for the cost surface: When the features differ in scale, the cost contours are long thin ovals: a tiny change in w1 changes the cost a lot, and a big change in w2 barely changes it. Gradient descent bounces across the narrow valley and crawls along it. After scaling, the contours are close to circles and the path goes almost straight to the minimum. (The picture is a simple bowl drawn to show the idea.)

title: 8.2 Three ways to rescale
text: 8.2 Three ways to rescale Ng's numbers: size has mean 600 and standard deviation 450, bedrooms have mean 2.3 and standard deviation 1.4. Method Formula Size (300 to 2000) becomes Bedrooms (0 to 5) becomes Divide by the maximum x / max 0.15 to 1 0 to 1 Mean normalization (x - mean) / (max - min) -0.18 to 0.82 -0.46 to 0.54 Z-score normalization (x - mean) / standard deviation -0.67 to 3.1 -1.6 to 1.9 Rule of thumb: aim for roughly -1 to +1 per feature. Anything from -3 to 3 or from -0.3 to 0.3 is fine. A feature from -100 to 100, one from -0.001 to 0.001, or body temperature at 98.6 to 105 degrees (all around 100) should be rescaled. There is almost never any harm in rescaling, so when in doubt, do it. Fit on training data only. Compute the mean and standard deviation from the training rows, and reuse those same numbers on validation, test and production data (Chapter 3). In scikit-learn that is StandardScaler().fit(X_train) and then .transform(...) for every set.

title: 8.3 It really does matter: an experiment
text: 8.3 It really does matter: an experiment Here is synthetic housing data built from a known recipe (price = 0.1 x size + 50 x bedrooms + 50, plus noise), fitted with the function from Chapter 7: rng = np.random.default_rng(1) size = rng.uniform(300, 2000, 200) beds = rng.integers(0, 6, 200).astype(float) y = 0.1 * size + 50 * beds + 50 + rng.normal(0, 10, 200) X = np.c_[size, beds] mu, sd = X.mean(axis=0), X.std(axis=0) Z = (X - mu) / sd # z-score each column w, b, h = gradient_descent(Z, y, alpha=0.1, steps=300) print(int(np.argmax(h <= h[-1] * 1.001)) + 1) # 68 steps to get within 0.1% of the final cost print(round(h[-1], 2)) # 39.11 final cost with scaling w2, b2, h2 = gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=1e-6, steps=300) # unscaled print(round(h2[-1])) # 5905 cost WITHOUT scaling after 300 steps With scaling, gradient descent is done in 68 steps and the cost is 39. Without scaling it is still at 5,905 after 300 steps, and it cannot use a bigger alpha, because any alpha above about 1.3e-6 makes it diverge. Same data, same model. Reading the weights after scaling. The weights from the scaled run are in scaled units. To get back to dollars per square foot, divide each by its standard deviation, and adjust b: print(np.round(w / sd, 3), round(b - np.sum(w * mu / sd), 2)) # [ 0.101 50.265] 48.96 A = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(y))] print(np.round(np.linalg.lstsq(A, y, rcond=None)[0], 3)) # [ 0.101 50.265 48.964] the exact answer The recipe was 0.1, 50 and 50, and both methods recover it up to the noise. Scaling changes how fast training is, not what it finds.

title: 8.4 Feature engineering
text: 8.4 Feature engineering Choosing or inventing the right features is often the biggest lever on quality (Ng, video 29). The idea: use what you know about the problem to combine or transform the raw columns so the pattern is easier to learn. Products and ratios. Ng's example: lot frontage x1 and depth x2 are less useful than their product x3 = x1 x2, the area. In lending: debt to income, loan to value, amount per term (amount divided by number of terms). Dates. A date becomes day of week, month, days since the account opened, days until the due date. Skewed numbers. Amounts and incomes are often skewed: a few huge values. Taking the logarithm often helps. Categories as numbers. A model needs numbers, so a category like loan purpose becomes one-hot columns: one 0 or 1 column per category. Do not number categories 1, 2, 3, because that would imply that home (3) is three times car (1). Missing values and outliers. Fill missing values with the median and add a column that says the value was missing; look at the extreme values before deciding whether they are errors or real. import pandas as pd offers = pd.DataFrame({ "OfferedAmount": [10000, 25000, 5000], "NumberOfTerms": [36, 60, 24], "Purpose": ["car", "home", "car"], }) offers["AmountPerTerm"] = (offers["OfferedAmount"] / offers["NumberOfTerms"]).round(1) offers = pd.get_dummies(offers, columns=["Purpose"], dtype=int) print(offers) # OfferedAmount NumberOfTerms AmountPerTerm Purpose_car Purpose_home # 0 10000 36 277.8 1 0 # 1 25000 60 416.7 0 1 # 2 5000 24 208.3 1 0

title: 8.5 Polynomial regression
text: 8.5 Polynomial regression A straight line fits curved data badly. The fix is to feed the same linear model extra columns made from powers of the feature (Ng, video 30): This is still linear regression, because the model is linear in the weights: the features are x, x squared and x cubed, and gradient descent does not care how they were made. Which shape? A quadratic eventually comes back down, which makes no sense for house prices. A cubic rises again for large houses. The square root of x flattens out but never goes down. Pick what fits the world you are modelling. Scaling is now essential. With size from 1 to 1,000, x squared reaches a million and x cubed a billion: from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline X = np.array([[300.0], [800.0], [1500.0], [2000.0]]) # size in square feet poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=3, include_bias=False) print(poly.fit_transform(X).max(axis=0)) # [2.e+03 4.e+06 8.e+09] the raw ranges Z = make_pipeline(poly, StandardScaler()).fit_transform(X) # all three columns now about -1.5 to 1.6 How many powers to use is a question about overfitting, which is the topic of Chapter 11. Choosing features properly, by measuring how well each choice performs on held-out data, comes in Ng's course 2. Loan example. The offers table has amounts in the thousands and terms in the tens, so scale them before gradient descent. Then add AmountPerTerm and compare the error with and without it. If the new feature helps, the model had a pattern it could not express with the raw columns alone. Common mistakes Scaling before splitting the data, which leaks test information into training. Not saving the training mean and standard deviation, then scaling new data with different numbers. Turning categories into 1, 2, 3. Adding polynomial features without scaling them. Check yourself Why does a feature measured in thousands make gradient descent slow? Z-score the value 1000 when the mean is 600 and the standard deviation is 450. Why is polynomial regression still called linear regression? Name two features you could build from the columns OfferedAmount and NumberOfTerms. Show answers (1) The weight for that feature must be tiny, and the cost surface becomes a narrow valley that gradient descent zigzags across. (2) (1000 - 600) / 450 = 0.89. (3) Because it is linear in the weights, even though the features are powers of x. (4) AmountPerTerm (amount divided by terms), and the logarithm of the amount. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 25 to 26 and 29 to 30 · the scikit-learn preprocessing guide · Google's Rules of Machine Learning , the sections on features.

title: Logistic regression, predicting yes or no
text: Purpose. Many business questions have a yes or no answer: will this customer repay, accept the offer, churn? Logistic regression is the standard first model for them. It is easy to explain, hard to beat as a baseline, and it is also the building block of neural networks. Key ideas Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification model. It outputs a probability between 0 and 1. It takes the same weighted sum as linear regression, z = w . x + b, and squeezes it through the sigmoid function. The decision boundary is where z = 0, which is where the probability is 0.5. The 0.5 cut-off is a choice, not a law. You can move it.

title: 9.1 Why not a straight line?
text: 9.1 Why not a straight line? Ng's example is a tumour that is benign (0) or malignant (1), predicted from its size. You could fit a straight line to those 0s and 1s and call anything above 0.5 malignant. It works on tidy data, but it breaks for two reasons (Ng, video 31): Add one very large tumour far to the right. The line tilts to chase it, the 0.5 crossing moves, and some tumours that were classified correctly are now wrong. One outlier should not rewrite your rule. The line produces numbers like -0.4 and 1.7. They are not probabilities and mean nothing. We need a curve that stays between 0 and 1 and flattens at both ends.

title: 9.2 The sigmoid
text: 9.2 The sigmoid For a very large z the sigmoid is close to 1. For a very large negative z it is close to 0. At z = 0 it is exactly 0.5. Some values: g(-3) = 0.047, g(-1) = 0.269, g(0) = 0.5, g(1) = 0.731, g(3) = 0.953. Read the model's output as a probability: if f(x) = 0.7, the model says there is a 70% chance that y = 1 for this input (and so a 30% chance that y = 0).

title: 9.3 The decision boundary
text: 9.3 The decision boundary To turn the probability into a yes or no, use a threshold, usually 0.5. The sigmoid is at least 0.5 exactly when z is at least 0, so the model predicts 1 when w . x + b is at least 0. The set of inputs where w . x + b = 0 is the decision boundary : a line when there are two features. Take w = [1, 1] and b = -3. The boundary is x1 + x2 = 3. Input x z = x1 + x2 - 3 Probability Prediction [1, 1] -1 0.269 0 [2, 2] 1 0.731 1 [3, 0] 0 0.5 on the boundary Straight boundaries are not the limit. If you feed the model squared features, such as x1 squared and x2 squared (Chapter 8), then with weights 1 and 1 and b = -1 the boundary x1 squared + x2 squared = 1 is a circle: points inside are class 0, points outside class 1. The model is still logistic regression; only the features changed.

title: 9.4 Odds and log-odds
text: 9.4 Odds and log-odds Beyond the videos (this is the statistician's view, as in StatQuest). The odds of an event are p divided by (1 - p): a probability of 0.8 is odds of 4 to 1. The logarithm of the odds is the log-odds (or logit): ln 4 = 1.386. Here is the neat fact: z = w . x + b is exactly the log-odds. Logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds, and the sigmoid just turns log-odds back into a probability. This gives you a way to read the weights: each increase of 1 in feature j multiplies the odds by e to the power w_j. A weight of 0.5 multiplies the odds by 1.649, so "4 to 1" becomes about "6.6 to 1", all else equal.

title: 9.5 The threshold is a choice
text: 9.5 The threshold is a choice The default 0.5 treats both mistakes as equally bad. In lending they are not. Approving a loan that defaults costs far more than declining a good applicant. You can lower the threshold to flag more risky cases (catching more bad loans, with more false alarms) or raise it to be stricter. Chapter 12 shows how to choose with numbers.

title: 9.6 More than two classes
text: 9.6 More than two classes Beyond the videos. With more than two classes (the Gmail tabs example) the sigmoid is replaced by the softmax function. It turns one score per class into probabilities that add up to 1. You will meet it again as the last layer of most neural networks. import numpy as np def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) print(sigmoid(np.array([-3, -1, 0, 1, 3])).round(3)) # [0.047 0.269 0.5 0.731 0.953] w, b = np.array([1.0, 1.0]), -3.0 for x in ([1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 0]): p = sigmoid(np.dot(w, x) + b) print(x, round(p, 3), "->", int(p >= 0.5)) # [1, 1] 0.269 -> 0 # [2, 2] 0.731 -> 1 # [3, 0] 0.5 -> 1 (exactly on the boundary: the >= rule says 1) p = 0.8 print(round(p / (1 - p), 2), round(np.log(p / (1 - p)), 3)) # 4.0 1.386 odds and log-odds Loan example. The probability that an offer is accepted is the sigmoid of w1 x amount + w2 x terms + w3 x credit score + b. A probability of 0.83 means "about 83 of 100 offers like this are accepted". You can rank offers by it, or turn it into a decision with a threshold, and a customer-facing explanation can use the weights: a larger amount lowers the odds of acceptance by a certain factor. Common mistakes Using linear regression on a 0 or 1 target. Thinking the model output is a certainty. It is a probability, and only as good as its calibration (Chapter 12). Treating 0.5 as sacred. Forgetting to scale the features before training (Chapter 8). Check yourself Compute sigmoid(0) and say what it means. For w = [2, -1], b = 1 and x = [1, 3], what is z, and what does the model predict? Why can a straight line not be the model for yes or no data? A probability is 0.2. What are the odds? Show answers (1) 0.5: the model is undecided, and the input is on the decision boundary. (2) z = 2 x 1 - 1 x 3 + 1 = 0, so the probability is 0.5, exactly on the boundary. (3) It gives values outside 0 and 1, and a single outlier can move its threshold. (4) 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25, which is 1 to 4. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 31 to 33 · StatQuest, Logistic Regression (9 minutes) and, for log-odds, Odds and Log(Odds), Clearly Explained · the scikit-learn logistic regression section .

title: Training logistic regression
text: Purpose. To use logistic regression you must find its weights. That needs a cost function that fits probabilities, then the same gradient descent as before. The surprise is how little changes. Key ideas Squared error is a bad cost for logistic regression: with a sigmoid it gives a bumpy surface. The right cost is the log loss. The log loss punishes a confident wrong answer very hard. The gradient has exactly the same form as for linear regression: (prediction minus target) times the feature. Only the prediction is now a sigmoid. At w = 0 and b = 0 the cost is always 0.693, the natural log of 2. This is a quick bug check.

title: 10.1 Why not squared error?
text: 10.1 Why not squared error? If you put the sigmoid inside the squared-error cost, the cost surface is no longer a single bowl: it has flat patches and traps, and gradient descent may get stuck. A different cost keeps the bowl shape (Ng, video 34).

title: 10.2 The loss on one example
text: 10.2 The loss on one example For one example with true label y and prediction f (a probability): If y = 1, the loss is -log(f). When f is near 1 the loss is near 0. When f is near 0 the loss explodes. If y = 0, the loss is -log(1 - f). The same, mirrored. True y Prediction f Loss Reading 1 0.9 0.105 right and confident: a small penalty 1 0.5 0.693 undecided 1 0.1 2.303 wrong and confident: a big penalty 0 0.1 0.105 right and confident 0 0.9 2.303 wrong and confident The model is encouraged to be right, and to be humble when it is unsure. Because y is either 0 or 1, the two cases fit in one line (Ng, video 35), and the cost J is the average of this loss over all m examples: When y is 1 the second term vanishes, and when y is 0 the first does, which gives the two cases above. At w = 0 and b = 0 every prediction is 0.5, so every loss is -log(0.5) = 0.693, and so is the average. If your code does not print 0.693 there, it has a bug.

title: 10.3 Where the log loss comes from
text: 10.3 Where the log loss comes from Beyond the videos (StatQuest's Logistic Regression Details Pt 2 shows it step by step). The log loss is maximum likelihood in disguise. The likelihood is the probability that the model assigned to exactly what happened: multiply f for every example with y = 1 and (1 - f) for every example with y = 0. The best parameters make that product as large as possible. A product of many small numbers is awkward, so take the logarithm, which turns it into a sum, and flip the sign so that "largest likelihood" becomes "smallest cost". The result is the cost above. So it is not an arbitrary choice: it is the principle of making the observed data as probable as possible.

title: 10.4 The gradient
text: 10.4 The gradient This looks exactly like the linear regression update from Chapter 7, and Ng points out how surprising that is. The difference is hidden inside f: for linear regression it is w . x + b, and here it is the sigmoid of w . x + b (Ng, video 36). It is not a coincidence: both come from the same family of models (generalized linear models), and the cost was designed that way.

title: 10.5 Code from scratch, checked against scikit-learn
text: 10.5 Code from scratch, checked against scikit-learn import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) def cost(w, b, X, y): f = sigmoid(X @ w + b) return -np.mean(y * np.log(f) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - f)) def fit(X, y, alpha=0.5, steps=5000): m, n = X.shape w, b = np.zeros(n), 0.0 for _ in range(steps): err = sigmoid(X @ w + b) - y # prediction minus target w = w - alpha * (X.T @ err) / m b = b - alpha * err.mean() return w, b rng = np.random.default_rng(2) X = rng.normal(size=(400, 2)) # two features, already on similar scales y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.7, 400) > 0.5).astype(float) print(round(cost(np.zeros(2), 0.0, X, y), 3)) # 0.693 w, b = fit(X, y) print(np.round(w, 3), round(b, 3)) # [2.617 2.412] -1.063 sk = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, tol=1e-10, max_iter=10000).fit(X, y) # C=inf means no regularization print(np.round(sk.coef_[0], 3), np.round(sk.intercept_[0], 3)) # [2.617 2.412] -1.063 pred = sigmoid(X @ w + b) >= 0.5 print(round((pred == y).mean(), 3), round(max(y.mean(), 1 - y.mean()), 3)) # 0.862 0.62 accuracy vs baseline The handmade model and scikit-learn agree to three decimals. The model gets 86.2% right against a baseline of 62% (always guessing the majority class). That is the comparison to make every time (Chapter 3). Note that this accuracy is on the training data. A fair score needs held-out data.

title: 10.6 In practice
text: 10.6 In practice Scale the features first (Chapter 8), or gradient descent will crawl. If one class is rare (defaults, fraud), accuracy is a poor yardstick; read Chapter 12. Add regularization when you have many features or little data (Chapter 11). scikit-learn's LogisticRegression has regularization on by default, with strength C , where C is 1 divided by lambda. For an unregularized fit, as above, pass C=np.inf . Loan example. Train a classifier on the offers table with label Accepted. Hold out 20% of the rows, scale with the training mean and standard deviation, fit your own function and scikit-learn on the same scaled features, and check that the weights agree. Then compare the held-out accuracy with the baseline of predicting the most common outcome. This is exactly the Wednesday drill of week 3. Common mistakes Using squared error as the cost. Writing log(0): if a prediction is exactly 0 or 1 and wrong, the loss is infinite. Libraries clip the values slightly away from 0 and 1. Reporting training accuracy as if it were the real score. Comparing your weights with scikit-learn's without setting the same regularization. Check yourself Compute the loss for y = 1 when f = 0.8, and for y = 0 when f = 0.8. Why is the cost exactly 0.693 at w = 0, b = 0? What changes between the gradient for linear and logistic regression? Why does log loss punish a confident wrong answer so hard, and is that desirable? Show answers (1) -ln(0.8) = 0.223 and -ln(0.2) = 1.609. (2) Every prediction is 0.5, and -ln(0.5) = 0.693 for either label. (3) Only the prediction f: a sigmoid in the logistic case. (4) The loss grows without limit as a wrong prediction approaches certainty. That is desirable, because it pushes the model to be calibrated: do not claim certainty you do not have. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 34 to 36 · StatQuest, Logistic Regression Details Pt 2: Maximum Likelihood · the scikit-learn page on linear models (see its logistic regression section for the exact cost it minimizes).

title: Overfitting, bias and variance, regularization
text: Purpose. The most common way a model fails is not that it learned too little, but that it learned the wrong thing: the noise in its training data. Understanding this failure, and the tools against it, is what separates a working model from a demo that falls apart on real data. Key ideas Underfitting (high bias): too simple, bad on training data and on new data. Overfitting (high variance): too flexible, great on training data, bad on new data. The test error is U-shaped as flexibility grows, while the training error only goes down. The gap between them is the warning sign. Regularization adds a penalty on large weights to the cost. It trades a little training accuracy for better behaviour on new data. The strength is lambda.

title: 11.1 Underfit, about right, overfit
text: 11.1 Underfit, about right, overfit The same fourteen noisy points, fitted three ways. The straight line is too simple: it misses the curve in the data ( underfitting ). The gentle curve follows the real pattern. The wiggly curve passes close to every dot, but between the dots it swings wildly, and it will predict badly for a new input ( overfitting ). Ng's housing version: a straight line does not follow the price curve, a quadratic is a reasonable fit, and a high-order polynomial hits every training house exactly and gives absurd prices in between. The goal is generalization : doing well on data the model has not seen. A model that memorizes its training set is like a student who learned last year's exam answers by heart. The same happens in classification. An overfit decision boundary twists around individual points; a good one is smooth.

title: 11.2 Bias and variance
text: 11.2 Bias and variance StatQuest's Bias and Variance video (7 minutes) gives the standard words for the two failures: Bias is the systematic miss of a model that is too simple to follow the true pattern. A straight line through a curve is wrong in the same way on every dataset. Variance is how much a model changes when you give it a different sample of data. A very flexible model fits whatever noise it was shown, so a different sample gives a very different curve. The figure averages 200 runs on data from a wavy curve plus noise. The test error is the error on new data. For a straight line (degree 1) it is 0.293, for a cubic (degree 3) it is 0.120, and for a degree 11 polynomial it is 0.372. At the same time the training error keeps falling, to 0.013 at degree 11. A model that scores nearly perfectly on its own training data can be the worst on new data. This is the bias-variance trade-off : simpler models have more bias and less variance, flexible ones the reverse, and the best model sits in between. Infinite Codes calls it the single most important idea in machine learning.

title: 11.3 Diagnosing which problem you have
text: 11.3 Diagnosing which problem you have Compare the error on the training set with the error on a validation set (Chapter 3). The numbers tell you which way you are wrong: Training error Validation error Diagnosis What to try High High, similar High bias (underfitting) More features, a more flexible model, less regularization Low Much higher High variance (overfitting) More data, fewer features, a simpler model, more regularization Low Low, similar Good Stop (Ng covers this properly in course 2, "advice for applying machine learning". For now, the habit is enough: always look at both numbers.)

title: 11.4 Three remedies for overfitting
text: 11.4 Three remedies for overfitting Collect more data. With many more examples the wiggly curve cannot pass through all of them. It is the best cure but often impossible. Use fewer features (or lower the polynomial degree). Pick the most relevant ones; this is called feature selection. A downside: you throw away information. Regularize. Keep all the features but stop any single weight from becoming huge (Ng, video 38).

title: 11.5 Regularization
text: 11.5 Regularization The wiggles of an overfit model come from large weights: the model needs big numbers to bend sharply. So add a penalty for large weights to the cost, and training has to balance fit against simplicity: The first term is the usual error: fit the data. The second is the new penalty: keep the weights small. lambda (a hyperparameter you choose) sets the balance. With lambda = 0 there is no penalty, and you are back to the original model. With a huge lambda the weights are pushed to almost zero and the model becomes nearly flat, which underfits. The bias b is usually not penalized (Ng, video 39). Dividing by 2m, as in the first term, keeps lambda comparable across datasets of different size. In gradient descent the only change is one extra term in the update of each weight (Ng, videos 40 and 41, for linear and logistic regression): Rearranged, it reads w_j (1 - alpha lambda / m) minus the usual step. On every iteration the weight is first shrunk by a tiny factor, and then moved as before. That is why this penalty is also called weight decay . For logistic regression the formula is identical; only f is the sigmoid.

title: 11.6 L2 and L1
text: 11.6 L2 and L1 Beyond the videos. The penalty above, the sum of squared weights, is called L2 regularization, or ridge . The alternative is L1 ( lasso ), which adds the sum of the absolute values of the weights. L1 tends to push some weights exactly to zero, so it also selects features. Elastic net mixes the two. StatQuest has short videos on each, and "Ridge vs Lasso, Visualized" shows why L1 gives zeros.

title: 11.7 Regularization in practice
text: 11.7 Regularization in practice In scikit-learn, lambda is called alpha in Ridge , and for LogisticRegression the setting is C , where C = 1 / lambda (small C means strong regularization). I checked both against a handmade gradient descent with the formulas above, and they match exactly. The experiment below fits a degree 10 polynomial to 15 noisy points with different regularization strengths, and averages over 200 random datasets: import numpy as np from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline rng = np.random.default_rng(11) truth = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x * 0.8) # the pattern we pretend not to know x_test = rng.uniform(0, 1, 2000) y_test = truth(x_test) + rng.normal(0, 0.25, 2000) alphas = [1e-6, 1e-2, 1, 100] # alpha is scikit-learn's name for lambda train_err = np.zeros(len(alphas)); test_err = np.zeros(len(alphas)) runs = 200 for _ in range(runs): # average over 200 small random datasets x = np.linspace(0, 1, 15) y = truth(x) + rng.normal(0, 0.25, 15) for i, a in enumerate(alphas): model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(10), StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=a)) model.fit(x[:, None], y) train_err[i] += np.mean((model.predict(x[:, None]) - y) ** 2) / runs test_err[i] += np.mean((model.predict(x_test[:, None]) - y_test) ** 2) / runs for a, tr, te in zip(alphas, train_err, test_err): print(f"alpha {a:<8} train error {tr:.3f} test error {te:.3f}") Alpha (lambda) Train error Test error Reading 0.000001 0.029 0.092 almost no penalty: fits the training data best, worse on new data 0.01 0.041 0.082 a little penalty: training error rises, test error falls 1 0.117 0.128 too much: starting to underfit 100 0.292 0.302 far too much: nearly flat, both errors high The lesson is in the shape: as lambda grows, the training error only rises, while the test error falls first and then rises. The noise in this data limits the best possible test error to about 0.06, so the gain from 0.092 to 0.082 is a real share of what was available. You choose lambda the same way you choose any hyperparameter: try several values and keep the one with the best validation error (Chapter 12), never the best training error. Loan example. Suppose you have 3,000 labelled applications and 60 candidate features, many of them overlapping (amount, amount per term, monthly cost, income, debt ratio). With so few rows and so many columns, an unregularized model will find accidental patterns. Regularization, plus a validation set to pick lambda, is the standard defence. A simple, strongly regularized logistic regression is a very hard baseline to beat on a table like this. Common mistakes Judging a model by training error alone. Choosing lambda by the test set (then the test set is no longer a fair judge). Forgetting to scale features before regularizing: the penalty treats all weights alike, so unscaled features are penalized unfairly. Making the model more flexible whenever it is wrong, without checking whether the error is bias or variance. Check yourself Your training error is 2% and your validation error is 18%. What is the problem and what are two remedies? What happens to the weights as lambda becomes very large? Why is a model that is perfect on its training data suspicious? In scikit-learn, which C corresponds to a lambda of 10? Show answers (1) High variance (overfitting). Remedies: more data, fewer features, a simpler model, more regularization. (2) They shrink towards zero and the model becomes almost flat (underfitting). (3) It may have memorized the noise, so it will probably do worse on new data. (4) C = 1 / 10 = 0.1. Go deeper: Ng, course 1, videos 37 to 41 · StatQuest, Machine Learning Fundamentals: Bias and Variance , Regularization Part 1: Ridge (20 minutes) and Ridge vs Lasso, Visualized (9 minutes) · the scikit-learn linear models guide , ridge and lasso sections.

title: Measuring a model
text: Purpose. A model is only as good as the evidence that it works. This chapter is about gathering that evidence honestly: which numbers to compute, on which data, and how to avoid fooling yourself. It is the same skill you will need to evaluate an LLM system. This chapter is almost entirely beyond the videos. It comes from standard practice and the scikit-learn documentation. Key ideas Accuracy can look great while the model is useless, whenever one class is rare. The confusion matrix counts the four kinds of outcome. Precision and recall each summarize one kind of error. A threshold trades precision for recall. Choose it with the real cost of each mistake. Evaluate on data the model has not seen, with cross-validation for small datasets and date-based splits for time-ordered ones. A predicted probability should match reality (calibration) when decisions depend on it.

title: 12.1 Why accuracy lies
text: 12.1 Why accuracy lies Take 1,000 loans, of which 50 defaulted. A "model" that predicts "no default" for everyone is 95% accurate and catches no defaulter at all. Accuracy hides the thing you care about, because defaults are rare. Whenever classes are imbalanced (fraud, defaults, rare diseases), look at the next measures instead.

title: 12.2 The confusion matrix
text: 12.2 The confusion matrix Suppose a model flags 60 loans as risky. Of its 60 flags, 35 really were defaults and 25 were good loans flagged by mistake. It missed 15 defaults. Everything else, 925 loans, was correctly left alone. Predicted: default Predicted: no default Actually default 35 (true positives, TP) 15 (false negatives, FN) Actually no default 25 (false positives, FP) 925 (true negatives, TN) Measure Formula Here In words Accuracy (TP + TN) / all 96% share of all answers that are right (the "always no" model gets 95%) Precision TP / (TP + FP) 58.3% of the loans I flagged, how many really were defaults Recall (sensitivity) TP / (TP + FN) 70% of the real defaults, how many I caught Specificity TN / (TN + FP) 97.4% of the good loans, how many I left alone F1 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall) 0.636 one number that is high only when both are high import numpy as np from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, accuracy_score y_true = np.array([1] * 50 + [0] * 950) # 1,000 loans, 50 defaulted y_pred = np.array([1] * 35 + [0] * 15 + [1] * 25 + [0] * 925) # flagged 35 of the 50, plus 25 good loans by mistake print(confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)) # [[925 25] # [ 15 35]] rows = truth (0, 1), columns = prediction (0, 1) print(accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred), round(precision_score(y_true, y_pred), 3), recall_score(y_true, y_pred), round(f1_score(y_true, y_pred), 3)) # 0.96 0.583 0.7 0.636 print(accuracy_score(y_true, np.zeros(1000)), recall_score(y_true, np.zeros(1000))) # 0.95 0.0 always "no default" The "always no default" model: accuracy 0.95, recall 0.0. Exactly the failure accuracy hides. Which mistake costs more? Suppose a missed default costs 5,000 euros and a wrongly flagged good loan costs 200 euros of lost margin (invented numbers). The model above costs 15 x 5,000 + 25 x 200 = 80,000 euros. Approving everyone costs 50 x 5,000 = 250,000 euros. The business question is never "is accuracy high" but "which mix of errors is cheapest".

title: 12.3 Thresholds
text: 12.3 Thresholds A classifier gives a probability, and the threshold turns it into a yes or no (Chapter 9). Moving it changes both numbers. On a held-out set of 80 cases (20% of the Chapter 10 data, scored by scikit-learn's default logistic regression): Threshold Cases flagged Precision Recall 0.3 39 0.72 0.93 0.5 30 0.77 0.77 0.7 18 0.83 0.50 A lower threshold flags more cases: it catches more of the real positives (higher recall) and makes more false alarms (lower precision). A higher threshold is stricter, with the reverse effect. Pick the threshold where the total cost is lowest. The ROC curve plots recall against the false alarm rate for every possible threshold, and its area ( AUC ) summarizes a model's ranking ability in one number: 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. This model's AUC is 0.915. For rare classes, a precision-recall curve is more informative than ROC.

title: 12.4 Metrics for regression
text: 12.4 Metrics for regression For numbers: MAE, RMSE and R squared (Chapter 5). Report the error in the original units, for example "typically 22 euros off", and compare it with the baseline of always predicting the average.

title: 12.5 Evaluating without fooling yourself
text: 12.5 Evaluating without fooling yourself Hold-out. Fit on the training set, score on a test set the model never touched. Use the test set once. Cross-validation. With little data, split into k parts (often 5), train on k - 1 parts, score on the remaining one, rotate, and average. It uses every row for testing exactly once and shows how much the score varies. Time-based splits. For loans and anything with dates, train on the past and test on the future. A random split lets the model learn from rows that are "after" the ones it is tested on. Leakage. Any feature that would not exist at decision time ruins all of the above (Chapter 3). from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X, y, cv=5, scoring="accuracy") print(scores.round(3), round(scores.mean(), 3)) # [0.838 0.875 0.875 0.85 0.888] 0.865 Five scores between 0.838 and 0.888: the spread is itself information.
